items.title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
items.excerpt: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work." The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications. items.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
items.excerpt: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword. Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript. Read full article Comments

items.title: ag-ui-protocol / ag-ui
items.excerpt: ### The open protocol that connects any agent to any app. **[Docs](https://docs.ag-ui.com)** · **[Examples](https://dojo.ag-ui.com)** · **[Spec](https://docs.ag-ui.com/spec/1.0)** · **[Discord](https://discord.gg/Jd3FzfdJa8)** **AG-UI is an open, lightweight, event-based protocol that standardizes how AI agents connect to user-facing applications.** Agents don't fit the request/response model. They stream tokens, call tools mid-response, update shared state, pause for a human, and spawn subagents, and every framework does it differently. AG-UI replaces that custom wiring with one bi-directional event stream: the agent emits typed events, and any client can render them, no matter which framework built the agent. The same agent can power a web app, a mobile app, a terminal, or Slack. > [!IMPORTANT] > **AG-UI 1.0 is here.** The protocol now has a stable, frozen [specification](https://docs.ag-ui.com/spec/1.0) backed by a JSON Schema, and the TypeScript, Python, and .NET SDKs are generated from it. 1.0 is backwards compatible in both directions: 0.x agents work with 1.0 clients and vice versa. items.title: BurntSushi / jiff
items.excerpt: Jiff ==== Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success. The focus of this library is providing high level datetime primitives that are difficult to misuse and have reasonable performance. Jiff supports automatic and seamless integration with the Time Zone Database, DST aware arithmetic and rounding, formatting and parsing zone aware datetimes losslessly, opt-in Serde support and a whole lot more. Jiff takes enormous inspiration from [Temporal], which is a [TC39] proposal to improve datetime handling in JavaScript. items.title: PrimeIntellect-ai / prime-agent
items.excerpt: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness Documentation • Verifiers • PRIME-RL Prime Agent is an open-source coding and research agent for general and long-running work. It is designed around two core abstractions: - The **[Recursive Language Model (RLM)](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/rlm)** treats context as variables (*prompt-as-a-variable*) and tools like recursive subagents as function calls (*programmatic tool /sub-agent calling*) inside a persistent REPL. - The **[Continual Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09998)** stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specifications as durable state that Prime Agent can refine through small, evidence-backed updates, local to the session by default. ## Install Install the latest stable version with the one-command installer: ```bash curl -fsSL https://app.primeintellect.ai/prime-agent/install.sh | sh ``` On Windows, install from PowerShell: ```powershell irm https://app.primeintellect.ai/prime-agent/install.ps1 | iex ``` The Windows installer downloads the latest stable Windows x64 build and verifies its checksum before installation. ## Why Prime Agent Prime Agent combines a persistent Python control environment with durable harness state, so useful working context and reusable operating patterns can outlive a single chat window. - **Everything is programmatic:** a persistent Python REPL is the built-in model tool; file operations, shell commands, tool use, subagents, and context…

items.excerpt: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. Some are through discount, some are uncapped, some have a fixed valuation cap, and some have both a discount and a valuation cap. - All safes (before first priced round) convert at the same time. items.title: My AI Agents Write Code Faster Than I Can Verify It
items.excerpt: 76% of developers and engineering managers in Sonar's 2027 State of Code report say they generate AI code faster than they can verify it! And I'm right there with them, since I run software factories where agents open pull requests around the clock. AI code looks correct way more often now, so the bugs that slip through are the subtle ones. The way I handle it in my own factories is simple. Agents can write whatever they want, but nothing merges until a check the agent doesn't control says it passes. The full report is really worth a read if you're handing more of your code to agents: https://fandf.co/4iN1mvB Thanks to Sonar for working with me on this!

items.title: I Trust My AI Agents to Merge Code… But NOT Ship It
items.excerpt: I trust my agents to merge code all night, but I definitely don't trust them to ship straight to production. Tests and reviews only tell you the code looks right. LaunchDarkly helps teams control and monitor how changes behave once they're live in production. They just launched Release Autopilot, where agents do the feature flag work that used to take an engineer: risk classification, success metrics, automatic release plans that start with a canary release, feature-level observability and flag cleanup. Safe, controlled releases with guardrails. Check out Release Autopilot: https://fandf.co/4sttJ6l Thanks to LaunchDarkly for working with me on this! #ad

items.title: Your Coding Agent Has a MASSIVE Blind Spot (You Need to Fix It)
items.excerpt: I've had agents break hundreds of times in production (sometimes in very embarrassing ways), and almost all the time it comes down to the blind spots in my coding agent. Your agent sees your code, but not what it does once it's running. The Dynatrace MCP Server brings live production data to the coding agent in your IDE, so you can ask about your running systems in plain language and trace a problem to the exact line behind it. Read the walkthrough: https://fandf.co/4ik3t9P Thanks to Dynatrace for sponsoring this video and working with me on it!

It flexibly transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials (ideas and experimental logs) into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including comprehensive literature synthesis and generated visuals, such as plots and conceptual diagrams. Acting like an orchestrated team of specialized agents, it handles outline generation, literature review, section writing, content refinement, and plotting to close the gap between raw research materials and submission ready papers. ## Key Features - **Multi-Agent Pipeline**: Orchestrates specialized agents (Outline, Literature Review, Section Writing, Content Refinement, Plotting) for end-to-end paper generation. - **Comprehensive Literature Synthesis**: Automatically searches, prioritizes, and integrates relevant literature into the manuscript. - **Visuals Generation**: Generates plots and supports the inclusion of conceptual diagrams. - **LaTeX Automation**: Produces submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts adhering to target conference templates. ## Installation 1. **Environment Setup**: The project relies on a Conda environment named `paper_orchestra`. items.title: Clear Signing Comes to Solana | Ledger's Ian Rogers
items.excerpt: BREAKING: Ledger brings Clear Signing to Solana, starting with Jupiter and Kamino It fixes a long-running problem called blind signing. Blind signing, in which users approve transactions displayed as unreadable data, has long been a weak point for hardware wallet users, since it leaves them unable to spot a malicious request. Rogers likened it to "signing a blank check". Clear Signing turns that data into plain words. S: So, where are we with adult intelligence amplification? T: Unfortunately, there aren't any clear pathways right now. There is no biotechnological intervention that we know of, where there's a clear argument that if you do that intervention, it would likely significantly increase the general cognitive capacities of an adult human. There are several approaches that are hopeworthy, but each one would be very expensive to pursue. S: What approach are you most hopeful about? T: On a strategy level, I'm most hopeful about more roadmapping work. Past drive-by efforts at roadmapping haven't worked. But it seems plausible that there are ways to significantly accelerate adult intelligence amplification, and it's just hard to tell what they are without thinking about it a bunch. So, I'd want us to collate a bunch of information about brains, intelligence, and various technical areas like brain-computer interfaces, brain surgery, brain genetics, neurophysiology, drugs, and so on. Then we'd ask big ambitious engineering questions with all that stuff at our fingertips, come up with ideas for how to do adult intelligence amplification, bounce ideas off each other and off of domain experts, break the ideas, go back to the drawing board, learn more, and so on. items.title: Curiosity as a Defense Mechanism Against Being Vulnerable
items.excerpt: When conversing with someone, there are two forms of curiosity you can use: epistemic and empathetic. Epistemic curiosity is an exploration of ideas by asking people ‘why’ they think something or ‘how’ they came to a conclusion. Empathetic curiosity seeks to understand the subjective thoughts and feelings people have based on their experiences. Both forms of curiosity, however, can be used as defense mechanisms against being vulnerable. When talking with a friend this week, we discussed how, sometimes, I use epistemic curiosity to endlessly ask people what they think about a topic. By making the conversation all about them, I get to avoid talking about myself. Why would I do that? It's because if I talk about myself, and they don’t like me, that rejection makes me experience the uncomfortable feeling of anxiety. My friend, on the other hand, admitted to often using empathetic curiosity, by repeatedly asking emotional questions to let people open up to her. Why? So that she can avoid talking about herself. Because again, if someone rejects who she is deep down, that will produce negative feelings. I’ve found that slowing down, and saying vulnerable things about myself , is making people feel closer to me. This felt terrifying at first, because they could reject my vulnerable self (this fear is likely due to evolutionary reasons of not wanting to be ostracized/abandoned, and left alone to die). But when you tolerate the feeling of anxiety and say vulnerable things anyway—ie…

items.title: The UK generates less wind power than Texas
items.excerpt: The United Kingdom generates less wind power than Texas every year, despite having over twice the population: (Texas data from ERCOT , UK data from OWID , code in the repo for this post .) I'm just irritated by people citing the UK as a major renewable energy success, always quoting relative numbers. Like: in 2025, 29% of UK electricity came from wind, how impressive. Well, in Texas it was 24%, but that's more impressive than 29% of UK electricity because the UK doesn't generate that much electricity. While the UK doesn't need as much electricity as Texas, because they don't have to air condition houses in the Texas heat, they need more than they're generating. They could use some air conditioning, first of all. They don't have dryers. Or, have them but don't run them, like this guy on r/AskUK , because of the electricity bill. There was a BBC article where they talked to a guy who had a heat pump installed, but went back to using the gas boiler, because it was so expensive to power the heat pump. This kind of thing is why Brits can't spin their low electricity use as enlightened and environmentally friendly. They have big plans for heat pumps, electric cars, hydrogen, but can't power them. So I'm irritated with those trumpeting the UK as a renewable energy success, but I'm also irritated with the opposition to wind. As if the issue is that in an insane spending spree, too many wind turbines were built, when really it is just not that much. These people blend in with the…

items.title: I'm worried about LLMs accelerating hardware for cheap ASI
items.excerpt: Basically: You could probably make a superintelligent AI with some currently unknown new paradigm for <$10k if you had the right hardware and algorithms Plausibly this would be much easier and faster with better hardware LLMs will make developers of novel-paradigm AI systems really good at hardware creation and design This seems bad, because those novel-paradigm AIs seem unlikely to be aligned with human values ASI could in principle be created cheaply I think it's very plausible that with the right hardware and algorithms someone could make a wildly superintelligent AI model extremely cheaply (<$10k in energy cost), for roughly the reasons described in this post (although I think it underestimates how useful hardware improvements will be for building ASI). Basically, I think that given that you can train a human from nothing to a 20-year-old for less than $10k worth of electricity, you should expect to be able to train an AI to a similar level for the same amount of electricity with the right hardware and algorithms. In fact you should be able to do that much more efficiently, since you only care about intelligence and don't need to worry about powering a whole human body. And if you're making your own brain it's probably pretty doable to just make it bigger. I don't think we'll get to this kind of novel ASI through iteratively improving current AI paradigms, but instead using something that's very different than current LLMs. To be clear, I also think that scaling LLMs…

items.title: AI Company Employees Should Unionize
items.excerpt: I. Should safety-conscious employees at AI companies quit in protest, or stay and fight? The latest argument didn’t resolve the dispute, but it did get me in contact with organizers working on both sides. Those planning to stay and fight are increasingly interested in labor organization. This doesn’t need to mean literal government-recognized Labor Unions. An existing group, Coalition Of Concerned AI Staff , is already helping support interested employees and investigating other models to do more. But it might involve using laws, rights, and tactics associated with the National Labor Relations Act and the labor movement. You may remember stories of bitter unionization battles at places like Starbucks, but AI workers can probably route around that. The toughest labor disputes happen in fields where the employer could easily fire all the organized workers and replace them from a bottomless pool of faceless scabs: although this is illegal, everyone needs to be maximally lawyered-up to prevent it. But there are so few skilled AI researchers that these laws are hardly necessary; if a dozen top AI researchers threaten to walk, it doesn’t matter whether Section P Sub-Section Q forces the AI company to negotiate - the AI company will want to negotiate. This cuts through the red tape that intimidates workers in less blessed fields 1 ; AI researchers could likely get away with only the package of rights provided by informal “concerted activity”, defined as two or more workers doing…

items.title: Escaping The “Outside Criticism” Trap
items.excerpt: I. Here’s a fun argument you can use to discredit anyone at any time. Start by calling them an arrogant fanatic with a totalizing ideology, someone who thinks they personally have solved all problems and can’t possibly learn from anyone who disagrees. If they have friends who agree with them, they’re a cult who collectively work to shelter themselves from any dissenting viewpoint. Then your victim responds by presenting one hundred notarized affadavits describing times when they have engaged with their critics, spent years studying books by their critics to see what they could learn from them, and even changed their beliefs in response to criticism. Then you spring the trap: “Ah, but you cherry-picked critics who operate within your worldview, a sort of loyal opposition. You continue to dismiss and exclude genuine critics who challenge your smug assumptions.” This always works. If your victim protests that they do like and appreciate many critics with worldviews different to theirs, you object that no, those guys are also within the system. You meant a different guy, even further away from their own view. Oh, they read that one too? You meant an even more different guy. Eventually, no matter how cosmopolitan they are, you will reach someone they actually don’t respect - let’s say a Stalinist pedophile who believes the Papacy is a Jewish plot - and then you go ha! I told you that you rejected everyone outside your little bubble! Everyone has people close to their ideology who…

Ask HN: Good ways to capture institutional knowledge?
items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: England were fired by Spain waving the World Cup around
items.excerpt: Spain vs England was a game that had almost everything, and may yet mean more; perhaps the most significant moment might have come before it had even started. The hosts took the opportunity of a first match back in Madrid since the World Cup to showcase the trophy, in what almost felt another homecoming. The mood was very much of revelling in their embossed status, something that would have had a particular edge for this specific nation. No country that has won the World Cup has waited as long for another trophy as England. And, as the 2010 winners Iker Casillas, Fernando Torres and Fernando Llorente presented Unai Simon that with that precious piece of brilliant gold, it was almost literally in England’s faces. items.title: How the Man City case could spark a drastic change in English football
items.excerpt: Over the past few weeks, those in Premier League boardrooms have noticed a very distinctive shift. The previous talk of trying to buy clubs, only for billionaires to realise how few are available, has gradually turned into talk of trying to sell clubs. Except, that is now even more difficult. The current calculation is that at least eight clubs - over a third of the league - are either officially or unofficially up for sale in some form. With some of these, there are actual prospectuses. With others, it’s that an ownership would be open to listening to offers. Some would consider full sales, others merely minority stakes. items.title: Why Emery should stay at Aston Villa and reject Manchester United
items.excerpt: It was the kind of thinking that used to govern most of football. A few years ago – although it could really have been many examples from the last 50 – a promising manager was being pursued by one of the game’s wealthiest clubs. He had built up a fine team with an upwardly mobile club, and it looked like they could be on the brink of something special… but that one thought wouldn’t go away. “These opportunities don’t always come along, so you have to seize them.” The manager ended up taking it, but not quite seizing it. He didn’t perform to the level required, albeit amid a lot of debate around the circumstances he walked into. His career has never reached the same heights, but the key point is that its trajectory was, in that moment of acceptance, drastically changed. The old thinking was wrong. That job just wasn’t right for him. He’s not the only one. There are a few examples, from Graham Potter to Julen Lopetegui, and there’s much more to it than just “backing yourself”. items.title: NEBench R1: a Reasoning Benchmark for Evaluating Nuclear Domain Competence in Large Language Models
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. items.title: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential…

items.title: How Much of SAR Vehicle Recognition Is the Vehicle? Background Shortcuts, Angle Gaps and Partial Libraries on MSTAR and ATRNet-STAR
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep networks score near 99% on the MSTAR vehicle benchmark, and the newer ATRNet-STAR benchmark was built to be harder. We ask how much of these scores comes from the vehicle itself. With a modern network (ConvNeXt-Small, 3 seeds) we first reproduce the known MSTAR result: with the central 96x96 pixels zeroed out, accuracy is still 73.3% (chance 10%). The same shortcut is present in ATRNet-STAR, which was collected across several scenes: with the vehicle removed, accuracy is 63.3% on the 40-class SOC split (chance 2.5%). Under the official scene-change split, the background stops helping and starts hurting. Accuracy is 22.8% on full chips and 30.8% when only the vehicle is shown. A SAR foundation model, SARATR-X, leans on the background more than ConvNeXt does (+4 to +6 points with the vehicle removed, in every seed) and does not solve the scene change. We then hold the amount of training data fixed and vary the depression angles used for training. Accuracy is set mainly by the gap to the nearest training angle: 57% at 15 degrees, 39% at 30 degrees and 26% at 45 degrees. Adding more training angles does not help. Finally, when most classes have training images at the test angle and a few do not, the missing classes do worse than when no class has them: 9.0% instead of 22.4% at a 45-degree gap. Most of their images are assigned to known classes. We recommend reporting background-only and target-only controls, and the angle gap…

items.title: Auditors Struggle to Catch Sabotage In End-to-End Transcripts of AI Safety Research
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we use a human expert as a proxy saboteur on AI safety research. We conduct a red-team/blue-team game where a human researcher runs AI safety experiments from scratch and auditors try to tell which were sabotaged and how. Given access to the full research transcript and the ability to run experiments, human auditors mostly fail to distinguish sabotaged from benign research: they achieve an AUROC of 0.59, not significantly better than chance, and fully identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases. Despite not being allowed to run experiments, the best frontier models outperform human auditors (Fable 5.1: AUROC 0.73, 32% full identification) within noise and weaker models perform comparably. When the saboteur chooses which experiments are attacked, rather than being required to sabotage every question given, sabotage identification drops further. Our results suggest that research sabotage by expert-level agents is difficult to detect with current auditing methods and provide a new setting for studying research sabotage.

items.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. items.title: Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
items.excerpt: AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap. Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers. Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren’t vulnerabilities at all. Another raw scan doesn’t help them. Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings. Maintainers are under intense pressure from this flood of reports. As Christian Grobmeier, a maintainer of Log4j, has put it, the AI defending open source has to be better than the AI attacking it . AI shouldn’t add to maintainers’ workload. So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings? GitHub and Microsoft are using Codename MDASH , Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world’s code is built on. The process Our pilot had two goals: send only findings that matter, and never send a maintainer an unverified finding. Here’s how it worked: Find. Codename MDASH , an AI system from Microsoft Security, scanned each project using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model and suggested fixes for what it found. Filter. items.title: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices
items.excerpt: Models are now good enough to work for hours or even days on their own. You don’t have to watch over every thing they do, but you still need to be able to check in, no matter where you are. An agent can’t live only inside one application. The work should continue even If you close a window or switch devices. In GitHub Copilot you can start an agent session in one place and pick it up in another. This session continuity runs on the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open standard built first in VS Code and adopted across GitHub. Here’s how it works, what we learned building it, and how you can use it to bring your agents into your own apps and workflows. At the same time, the Copilot app was being developed, alongside the existing GitHub mobile apps for iOS and Android. Each product was doing its own distinct integration with cloud-based agents to work towards delivering session continuity. Each of these integrations solved the problem for one product, but…

items.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
items.excerpt: How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline. An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database. I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” . Define one job and when it applies A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. items.title: Sudan: Devastating RSF drone strikes on civilians in El Obeid should be investigated as war crimes
items.excerpt: Country: Sudan Source: Amnesty International Please refer to the attached file. Drone strikes by Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which hit residential areas and civilian infrastructure in El Obeid city, in Sudan’s North Kordofan State, killing dozens and disrupting essential services, should be investigated as war crimes, Amnesty International said today. The organization investigated nine RSF drone strikes in El Obeid and its surroundings, which killed 37 civilians and injured 10 between June and August 2026. Three of the strikes hit residential areas; four struck key civilian infrastructure, including El Obeid’s power plant, fuel stations, and the main market; and two targeted moving vehicles. In all incidents, interviewees said they either saw or heard the drones, moments before or after the strikes. Amnesty International’s investigation did not identify military objectives in the vicinity of the sites at the time they were struck. El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan State, remains under the control of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and their allied forces. items.title: Scientists say this pesticide needs a warning label for pollinators
items.excerpt: Of the many chemicals humans have invented to control agricultural pests, some of the most devious are called “ insect growth regulators .” As the name suggests, these compounds don’t kill insects directly; they alter their development so they can’t grow into healthy, reproducing adults. This makes insect growth regulators a remarkably useful tool for taming populations of insects like whiteflies and mealybugs, which can spread diseases and sap nutrients out of food crops. There’s just one problem: Farmers don’t want to regulate all insects in this way. Beneficial insects like honey bees risk getting caught in the crosshairs of these chemicals, to the detriment of farmers who need their pollination services to produce crops like pears and cherries. One insect growth regulator in particular has emerged as a potential issue for pollinators: buprofezin. Ongoing research out of Washington State University, or WSU, suggests that buprofezin may be hazardous to honey bees even at concentrations 10 times below those commonly found in pollen. A study published in 2024 connected the compound to “severe brood mortality.” At a meeting of the Washington State Beekeeping Association last month, WSU entomology professor Brandon Hopkins said buprofezin products should be sold with a pollinator warning — a break from current requirements of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, or EPA. In many situations it took the form of campaigns of civil resistance aimed at achieving change through nonviolent forms of resistance. In some situations it was accompanied, or followed, by civil unrest and armed rebellion. The process was long and tenuous in many countries, and many of these movements did not fully achieve their goals, although the efforts of these movements did lead to improvements in the legal rights of previously oppressed groups of people.
